Carta sales rep reached out unsolicited to a family member/angel investor whose investment was never publicized, at exactly the company's Series B share price, raising concerns Carta used confidential cap table data to solicit secondary sales.
I went with Pulley after a Carta sales rep called me out of the blue, on a number they must have scraped from an SEC filing, ignoring the do-not-call registry.

Carta announced it would exit its secondary trading business after backlash, but commenters noted this didn't address deeper questions about how broadly employee access to customer cap table data had been abused.

Carta was charging me $8,000 per year. I found an alternative (Cake Equity) with all the features for 10% of the price. It took multiple calls with a rep to cancel because Carta did not want to add an easy cancel option.

Carta's cancellation process requires a meeting with a customer success rep before you can cancel, and founders report being unable to schedule that meeting or reach a human, effectively trapping them in the subscription.

After leaving my company I exercised options for ~$20k; six months later Carta attempted a single bank transfer, it failed and overdrafted me, and they permanently canceled my option exercise rights with no second attempt or warning.

I'm the founder of Eqvista, a Carta competitor; we've seen significant migrations from Carta due to cost, lengthy 409A valuation timelines, difficulty accessing support, and how hard Carta makes it to cancel and transfer your cap table elsewhere.
Paul Graham (2021): 'If you use Carta to manage your cap table, they will spam all your investors.'

A founder asked whether switching from a free cap table tool to Carta would be painful, noting Carta onboarding 'has an involved process and associated fees' with dozens of help articles just for onboarding private companies.
